If Trump Can’t Fill a Dallas Arena, Can He Turn Out a November Vote?
 
Plus, the Iran war could last through the end of Trump’s second term, and Witkoff earned more than $100 million last year from the president’s crypto firm
 
 
JIM LO SCALZO/EPA/SHUTTERSTOCK
 

Good morning from Dallas. There were scores of empty seats in the upper tiers of the American Airlines Center for President Trump’s keynote address at the Republican convention. And there were plenty of empty seats in the lower sections too.

 

It was a five-hour drumroll of speakers leading up to the president’s remarks, but those seats never filled.

 

The floor of the arena was rocking. That, in essence, represents his base of supporters. But those upper tiers and some of the other sections represent the difference makers in November. And they didn’t show up.

 

This, in a nutshell, is the test Trump and Republicans face heading into the November midterms. They need to, more than metaphorically, fill those seats.

 

“Pretend I’m on the ballot,” Trump told the arena during his speech, acknowledging that midterm elections can prove difficult for the party that controls the White House.

 

His speech was up-tempo and he had plenty of laugh lines, but can that be enough? He also promised all American adults a $5,000 “dividend” after the election if Republicans retain control of Congress.

 

The crowd’s awkward booing of Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R., S.D.) halfway through Trump’s speech hinted at the tension.

 

During the first day of the two-day convention, speaker after speaker implored Republicans to turn out to vote and turn back Democrats. (Democrats have plenty of their own problems and remain a very divided party).

 

“If Democrats take over one chamber of Congress, the [Trump] agenda stops,” RNC Chairman Joe Gruters said early in the event. “We’re sure as hell not going to let that happen.”

 

“These people are sick,” Rep. Tom Emmer (R., Minn.) said of Democrats.

 

“They hate our culture,” Sen. Tim Scott (R., S.C.) said.

 

“America, it’s time for choosing,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said shortly before Trump took the stage.

 

On Wednesday night, Trump was competing with opening night of the NFL, record-high gas prices, scorching Dallas heat and millions of frazzled parents juggling back-to-school responsibilities. Those are some big headwinds.

 

He has won elections in the past by bottling energy and then unleashing that on Election Day. He still has time to find that enthusiasm.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

RNC Midterm Convention Night 2: Sen. Ted Cruz (R., Texas), House Speaker Mike Johnson (R., La.), Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., former press secretary Karoline Leavitt and Vice President JD Vance are set to take the stage this evening in Dallas.

 

South Korea: The South Korean government is nearing the announcement of a major energy investment project in the U.S. to support America’s AI build-out.

 

Dan J. Sullivan Jr.: The Alaskan retiree’s sudden interest in the Senate race has created a conundrum for Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, who is waging a close battle with Democratic challenger Mary Peltola.

 

Charlie Kirk: Today marks the first anniversary of Kirk’s murder at a Turning Point USA event in Utah.

 

Trump’s Thursday: The president will tour the National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas, at 1 p.m. ET. He will attend the second night of the RNC Midterm Convention this evening, where he gives closing remarks at 9:45 p.m. ET.

What I’m Following

 
 
VALENTYN OGIRENKO/REUTERS
 

The White House has confronted the possibility that the Iran War will last through the end of Trump’s presidency. The administration is preparing to maintain its Iran blockade indefinitely, which has led the president’s top aides to raise the possibility that the war might last through the end of Trump’s term in January 2029. Trump on Wednesday said the war would end after November’s midterm elections.

 

Steve Witkoff earned more than $100 million from an entity tied to a Trump crypto firm. The Middle East envoy’s income surged in 2025, lifted by gains from the entity that owns his stake in World Liberty Financial, according to a new financial disclosure. That income included nearly $69 million in cash and $38 million in crypto, according to the filing.

 

Rhode Island’s governor was soundly defeated in his state’s Democratic primary. Gov. Dan McKee is the first sitting U.S. governor to lose a primary contest in nearly a decade. The winner, former CVS executive Helena Buonanno Foulkes, will be favored in the November election in the Democratic-friendly state.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Iran is showing a new appetite for escalation as its forces take aim at the U.S. Navy in a way they haven’t done since the start of the war.

 

• The Trump administration is proposing an overhaul of the 2030 census by eliminating questions about race and restricting how immigrants would be counted when census results are used for allotting congressional seats.

 

• The U.S. is relying on fusion breakthroughs to turbocharge its nuclear weapons arsenal amid three-way battle with Russia and China.
